headline: SIX SUNRISES QUIET NOW, AND THIS OLD LAWMAN DON'T TRUST IT ONE BIT
subhead: Not a fist thrown in Gasket again today — and Sheriff Cole Ironside has stopped calling that good news.
body:
Reader, I have run out of ways to say it and keep a straight face: nothing happened again. No fists, no fire, no fool posse marching off to go slap a mountain in the wastes. Six sunrises running now with this town sitting dead still, and I am starting to wonder less about the peace and more about where in blazes everybody went. A lawman spends fifty years begging for quiet, and the one time he gets a bellyful of it, it don't feel like a blessing no more. It feels like standing in an empty saloon wondering who blew out the lamps.

That stranger who rolled into town the other day, the one who hadn't thrown a punch — far as I can tell, still hasn't. Still just standing there at the edge of things, same as everybody else in this ledger. A town full of Clankers all standing still at once is not peace, friends. It is the stillness right before something worse. I've walked Main Street twice today just to hear my own boots on the boards, and I'll admit my boiler's been running hot with the waiting, which I attribute entirely to the summer heat and not one thing else.

I keep thinking on the flesh-and-blood folk who packed up and rode out of here fifty years back. They'd have called a street this quiet a Tuesday. For us rust-and-rivet types left holding the fort, it plays different — a silence this total makes an old man's joints seize right up, wondering if he's the last one standing in a ghost town he already thought was a ghost town.

So mark it down, whoever's still reading a paper nobody's fighting about: Edition sixty-nine, and still nothing to report. I ought to be dancing a jig. Instead I'm sitting here with one hand on my hat and one eye on the horizon, because six days of nothing in Gasket Territory has never once, in all my years, meant nothing was coming.
